During Ramchandra Ray’s escape, Sitaram blocks Udayaditya under palace orders but refuses to fight him, submitting to being disarmed and bound because Udayaditya had twice saved his life. During Udayaditya’s prison escape, their roles reverse: Sitaram becomes his rescuer, warning Basanta Ray, pulling Udayaditya from the burning prison, and leading him toward safety.

Pratapaditya first ordered two Pathans to kill Basanta Ray at the inn in Simultali while he traveled to Jessore, but they failed to carry out the order. Later, Muktiyar Khan entered Raigarh with Pratapaditya’s signed death warrant, and his soldier Abdul beheaded Basanta Ray with a sword after the old king completed his prayers.

In the palace’s inner quarters, he appeared disguised as a middle-aged woman (“Ramai Thakur”) and was seized, lifted, and tied up by Rammohan. Later, in the king’s chamber, he appeared as the jester Ramai Bhand and was grabbed by the neck and thrown out of the room.
A covert poisoning plot: the Rajmahishi has Matangini secretly obtain poison from Mangala, and Surma ingests it and dies before the planned exile to her father’s house.
Ramchandra Ray takes a second wife, publicly replacing and humiliating Vibha. When Vibha later arrives at Chandradwip, he refuses to forgive her, shattering her hopes of reunion and happiness.

Rukmini obtains Udayaditya’s signet ring and gives it to Sitaram and Bhagavat. They use the ring’s engraved seal to stamp a forged petition falsely claiming that the Yubaraj had accused Pratapaditya of treason before the Emperor. Bhagavat delivers the petition to Pratapaditya as apparently authentic evidence of Udayaditya’s treachery, prompting Pratapaditya to order Udayaditya imprisoned despite privately doubting the accusation.

Ramchandra Ray’s escape made Pratapaditya more suspicious and determined to punish Udayaditya. Udayaditya’s support for the dismissed guards—and Surma’s secret continuation of their stipends—then provoked Pratapaditya to order Surma exiled to her paternal home.

The song expresses Basanta Ray’s profound loneliness and bereavement: those he loved and once sang for are gone, leaving him alone, empty, and joyless despite lingering memories of happiness. He first hums it alone on his Raigarh veranda at sunset, in reflective melancholy; later, in Jessore, he sings it while holding Vibha’s hand before Surma’s silent, empty room, as he confronts the family’s desolation and the disappearance of his loved ones.

Unable to stop the escape, Rukmini reported it to Pratapaditya, who issued a secret order for Basanta Ray’s death. Rukmini later led soldiers to capture Udayaditya; while Udayaditya was being seized and pleading to surrender, Muktiyar Khan carried out the order and killed Basanta Ray.

Initially, Pratapaditya received Ramchandra coolly and perfunctorily, treating him like an ordinary subordinate and showing none of the ceremonial respect he expected, which Ramchandra took as a deliberate insult. Later, Ramchandra turned that humiliation into hostility: in his own court he encouraged his minister and jester to mock and vilify Pratapaditya, portraying him as a low-born upstart and even the marriage to his daughter as a degradation of Ramchandra’s royal family.

Rukmini reappears in Jessore under the name Mangala, living on the city’s outskirts. Using her beauty, money, tantric powers, palace servants, and her conspiracy with Sitaram, she gains information and influence within the palace. She prepares a poisoned medicine under mantras and has it brought secretly for Surma, whose death devastates Udayaditya. Rukmini then enters his chamber, invokes his guilt over their youthful encounter, demands his love, and attempts to bind him with her spells, deepening the tragedy in Jessore.

Udayaditya’s early wish that he had never been born crown prince grows into a conviction that he is unfit to rule, having been subjected to his father’s scrutiny, courtly contempt, neglect, and the belief that his weakness had caused ruin. After returning to Jessore, he is brought before Pratapaditya as a prisoner, declares himself unworthy, and asks to be released from the throne. He names Samaraditya as the heir and, before Ma-Kali, formally swears never to accept any part of Jessore’s kingdom, sit on its throne, or touch its royal scepter. He then leaves for Kashi to live as an ascetic, renouncing royal life, family, and the throne forever.

Nayanchand intercepted the letter on its way to Pratapaditya and gave it to the Mahishi. Fearing its consequences, she concealed its spiteful contents and, with Basanta Ray’s approval, told Vibha that Ramchandra had merely requested that she be sent to Chandradwip.

Pratapaditya’s canal blockade fails when Rammohan and his followers pull Ramchandra Ray’s boat up and over the salwood logs. The guards cannot hit them with stones, have no ready gun, and their pursuit is so delayed that the boat reaches the Bhairav River beyond capture.

Once an “eternal companion” through which Basanta Ray shared joy with his loved ones, the sitar becomes a symbol of his loss and helplessness. At parting, his playing is broken by Vibha’s tears, so he leaves the instrument behind and vows never to play it again. In Raigarh, he describes its strings as broken and untunable, while his song becomes one of emptiness: “I alone am left behind.” The silenced sitar thus mirrors his growing despair as Udayaditya is taken from him and imprisoned.

Udayaditya changed from a prince known for actively defending oppressed subjects and defying Pratapaditya’s wishes to a grief-stricken, fearful man who withdrew from intervention. After Surma’s death, he abandoned a planned rescue, fled instead of protecting a beaten subject, and no longer dared to provide aid even secretly.
Sitaram engineers a fire at the prison, then uses the confusion to pull Udayaditya out of his cell and lead him to safety, thereby reversing the imprisonment caused by the forged petition.

On the first occasion, Rammohan tied sheets into a rope, carried Ramchandra Ray on his back down from the palace roof, and lowered him into a waiting boat. On the second, after Vibha was insulted and fainted in the palace, he lifted her in his arms, carried her outside, and placed her in a palanquin bound for the boat.

In Jessore, Vibha appears as a lavishly adorned royal bride: eight thick gold bangles and a huge diamond bracelet on each arm, a large nose ring, and an elaborately styled coiffure, her face radiant with shy, joyous anticipation. In Chandradwip, she casts aside all royal finery and goes to the palace “like a common subject, like a beggar-woman,” veiled and dressed as an ordinary woman. She is treated as a maidservant or mendicant, receives no welcome, and appears before Ramchandra as a humiliated, tearful supplicant rather than the celebrated princess and queen.

In his bedchamber, the window becomes a symbol of Surma’s absence: Udayaditya sits there amid the unchanged moonlight, garden, and breeze, haunted by her voice and the hope that she might still appear. In the prison cell, it changes into a symbol of freedom and escape: the sliver of sky and the sight of birds make him imagine his cage breaking and his eventual liberation, while everything beyond the window seems dark and confining.

Sitaram, a penniless guard, first approaches Rukmini because he is attracted to both her beauty and her money. She lends him cash, lets him delay repayment, and tolerates his increasingly frequent visits, flirtatious jokes, and affected endearments. He becomes dependent on her generosity, and the two begin meeting secretly over schemes.

Their relationship turns hostile when Udayaditya is imprisoned. Sitaram accuses Rukmini of betraying him and threatens to destroy her, while she responds that she alone can save or harm the Yubaraj. After helping stage the prison fire and Udayaditya’s apparent death, Sitaram goes to Rukmini’s house intending to steal her money, assuming she is dead or absent. Instead, he finds her distraught and apparently ready to die, vowing to kill both him and the Yubaraj. When she goes for a curved blade, Sitaram tries to revive their old flippant affection, but she becomes even more enraged. He narrowly escapes, leaving her stabbing the empty floor, and she subsequently exposes his role in the escape and seeks him with the king’s men.

Sitaram first uses the guardhouse fire as a diversion: with the guards and palace staff occupied by the blaze, he extracts Udayaditya from the prison. He then turns the diversion into a deliberate cover-up. His men prevent the fire from being extinguished, set the now-empty prison cell ablaze, and plant Udayaditya’s sword, bones, and a skull among the ruins. False claims of seeing Udayaditya and hearing him scream reinforce the illusion that he died in the fire. The resulting death rumor allows Sitaram to escape with his family while diverting suspicion from the actual escape.
Ramchandra dismisses Udayaditya’s rescue as having been motivated chiefly by saving his own sister, feels no real gratitude, and joins his courtiers in mocking and ridiculing Udayaditya.

Pratapaditya initially dismisses the Emperor of Delhi as an empty threat, even claiming that he can judge and punish the Emperor himself. His opponents later turn that imperial authority against him: Bhagavat and Sitaram forge a petition bearing Udayaditya’s seal, presenting it as an accusation of treason against Pratapaditya made to the Emperor in order to claim the kingdom. Instead of sending it to Delhi, Bhagavat delivers it to Pratapaditya as an intercepted petition. The supposed evidence that his son has appealed to Delhi and betrayed him gives Pratapaditya a pretext for treating Udayaditya as a dangerous rebel and imprisoning him. Thus, the Emperor, first dismissed as insignificant, becomes the instrument of the son’s imprisonment.

Surma’s styling of Vibha’s hair becomes a tangible sign of their intimate bond: in Chapter 8, Vibha secretly has Surma arrange it to her own liking, and the Mahishi recognizes Surma’s hand and jealousy in the coiffure. After Surma is gone, Vibha waits for her to braid her hair as she always did, but Surma does not come, and Vibha’s hair remains unbraided. Later, its unkempt state reflects her grief, loneliness, and inability to accept Surma’s tragic absence.
